endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: AI training restriction: If the vendor is not permitted to train or fine-tune models on your data, this must be stated explicitly.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Da ta and prompts contributed by users should primarily be used by developers to improve the user experience and AI tool quality and not simply increase the AI tool’s market value or revenue generating potential.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this recommendation tests whether explicit contract terms on vendor training or fine-tuning change how vendors use organizational data and prompts, and no study documents how often unauthorized use occurs. The recommendation rests on two endorsements, one framework that states it as a requirement and one guidance document that states it as an expectation.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The support consists of expert consensus from two sources, which reflects professional judgment and does not show that contract language changes vendor behavior or patient outcomes.

The CHAI playbook uses mandatory language and says a prohibition on training must be stated explicitly. The augmented intelligence principles say user data and prompts should primarily serve tool quality and user experience rather than vendor revenue. The two sources agree on direction but differ in strength, and neither reports how the terms are enforced.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared vendor agreements with and without explicit training and fine-tuning clauses to measure effects on vendor data use, audit findings, breach or misuse events, or negotiated benefit to the organization. Studies that audit actual vendor practices against contract terms would establish whether the hazard occurs and whether the clause reduces it.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net organizations may have less negotiating power with vendors, and whether they can secure these contract terms, and with what effect, remains unmeasured.
